A graphic posted on October 15th ranked 186 franchises by win percentage across the 2020s — NBA, NFL, MLB, NHL, MLS, NWSL, and WNBA — and pulled 148K views. The concept is worth taking seriously. Three measurement problems make the current version harder to interpret than it looks.

**Cross-sport win percentages are not on the same scale.** MLB win percentages cluster tightly around .500 by design: 162 games, high parity, mean reversion over a long season. The NFL spreads much wider with 17 games and higher variance per result. A team at 58% in the NFL is roughly 2 standard deviations above its league mean; the same figure in MLB is about 1.2. Ranking them together sorts by league structure as much as by team quality. I standardized each team's win percentage to its league distribution — that version of the ranking looks quite different from the raw one.

**Expansion franchises need a tenure correction.** The Golden State Valkyries appear at #11 overall after roughly 1.4 seasons. With that sample, the standard error on their win percentage is nearly twice what it is for a franchise with a full window. The yellow border in the graphic flags new teams, but it doesn't tell you how much to shrink the estimate. A simple tenure-weighted adjustment — shrinking short-window franchises toward the league mean in proportion to their sample size — moves the Valkyries' effective estimate closer to the middle of the WNBA distribution, which is the honest read.

**The most interesting question is invisible: who converts wins into championships?** Consider the NFL:

| Team | Win% | Titles | Finals appearances |
|:-----|-----:|------:|------------------:|
| Buffalo Bills | 73.3% | 0 | 0 |
| Kansas City Chiefs | 72.4% | 3 | 5 |

The Bills have a *higher* win percentage than the Chiefs. The Chiefs have three Super Bowl titles. That inversion — and how common or rare it is across leagues — is the most analytically interesting thing in the data. The same pattern shows up in the NHL: the Boston Bruins (59.6%, zero Cups) sit just above the Florida Panthers (58.4%, two Cups) and the Edmonton Oilers (58.5%, zero Cups despite back-to-back Finals appearances in 2024 and 2025).

The follow-up post will show per-league panels with tenure-corrected estimates, a win% vs. championships scatter, and a look at which franchises are most and least efficient at converting regular-season dominance into hardware. The data is [already compiled](/posts/blog/sports-wins-2020s/) — 186 teams, seven leagues, titles and Finals appearances for the full 2020s window.
